introduction: Xenophon, Memorabilia 4.2.24–30; introductory context 4.2.1–8. Read this controlled course adaptation with the glosses, then revisit its source and historical setting on page three.

The books, Delphic maxim, and examination of ability follow the source. The two-tablet classroom exercise is explicitly supplied to practice -όω verbs and numbers; it is not a report about Euthydemus.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Εὐθύδημος πολλὰ βιβλία εἶχεν. σοφὸς εἶναι ἐνόμιζεν καὶ λέγειν καὶ πράττειν ἐβούλετο. ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης αὐτῷ διελέγετο καὶ τὴν γνώμην αὐτοῦ ἐξήταζεν.
Ὁ Σωκράτης ἐρωτᾷ· «ἐν Δελφοῖς τὰ γράμματα εἶδες;» ὁ δὲ Εὐθύδημος ὁμολογεῖ. τὰ γράμματα λέγει· «γνῶθι σεαυτόν.» ἡ δὲ ἐρώτησις οὐκ ὀλίγον ἔργον παρέχει.
Τὸ ὄνομα μόνον οὐ δηλοῖ τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. ὁ ἵππον ζητῶν οὐ τὸ ὄνομα μόνον σκοπεῖ. τὸν ἵππον ἐξετάζει· ταχὺς ἢ βραδύς ἐστιν;
Οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἔργα σκοπεῖ. ὁ μὲν ἑαυτὸν γιγνώσκων τὰ χρήσιμα ζητεῖ. ὁ δὲ οὐ γιγνώσκων πολλάκις ἁμαρτάνει· ἡ ἐλπὶς οὐ πᾶν ἔργον κατορθοῖ.
Ἐν τῇ ἀσκήσει δύο πίνακας πληροῦμεν. ἐν μὲν τῷ πρώτῳ τὰ ἔργα γράφομεν, ἐν δὲ τῷ δευτέρῳ τὰ τεκμήρια. οὐ χρυσοῦς πίναξ ἀληθῆ γνώμην παρέχει.
«Ὡς ἐγὼ νομίζω, σοφός εἰμι» οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστι τῷ «τὸ ἔργον ὀρθῶς πράττω». τίνα οὖν τεκμήρια ζητοῦμεν; ὁ Σωκράτης οὐ μόνον τὸν λόγον ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν βίον ἐξετάζει.

reading.translation:
Euthydemus had many books. He thought he was wise and wished to speak and act. Socrates conversed with him and examined his judgment.

Socrates asks, “Did you see the inscription at Delphi?” Euthydemus agrees. The inscription says, “Know yourself.” The question presents no small task.

The name alone does not reveal a person’s ability. Someone looking for a horse does not consider only its name. He examines the horse: is it fast or slow?

In the same way a person examines his own actions. Someone who knows himself seeks useful things. Someone who does not know often makes mistakes; hope does not make every undertaking succeed.

In the exercise we fill two tablets. On the first we write the tasks, and on the second the evidence. A golden tablet does not provide a true judgment.

“As I think, I am wise” is not the same as “I do the task correctly.” What evidence, then, do we seek? Socrates examines not only speech but also life.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — νοῦς: a mind at work

blocks.title: νοῦς: a mind at work
body: νοῦς names mind or understanding. Its contracted forms, such as νοῦ and νοῦν, reward attention to articles and case. The word is not a label for a number of books.

δηλόω, “make clear,” describes something a good explanation does. Put the two together conceptually: learning should make a relation clear to the mind, rather than merely add an object to a collection.

grammar.intro: Read each explanation and reference table, then practice the topic before the required grammar check. Supplementary examples are course compositions; they do not add historical incidents to Xenophon’s account.
objectives: Explain and apply Contract verbs in -όω.

sections.title: 1. Contract verbs in -όω
body: In -όω verbs, ο contracts with following vowels: δηλόω becomes δηλῶ, δηλόεις becomes δηλοῖς. Present infinitive δηλοῦν comes from δηλόειν. Read the contraction before deciding person and number.

The imperfect adds the augment before the contracted stem: ἐδήλουν, ἐδήλους, ἐδήλου. ἐδήλουν can be first singular or third plural. These verbs provide useful language for making something clear and judging something worthy.

sections.title: 2. Contract second-declension nouns
body: Contract nouns bring adjacent vowels together in the noun stem and ending. νοῦς, νοῦ, “mind,” and πλοῦς, πλοῦ, “voyage,” preserve familiar second-declension cases under contracted spellings.
Use the article to check the result: τὸν νοῦν is accusative; τῷ νῷ is dative. The circumflex often marks a contraction. Do not mistake νοῦν for an infinitive simply because both may end in -οῦν.

sections.title: 3. Numbers and measured claims
body: One, two, three, and four require special attention. εἷς/μία/ἕν has three genders; τρεῖς is masculine/feminine, τρία neuter; τέτταρες is masculine/feminine, τέτταρα neuter. Most cardinal numbers from five through one hundred are indeclinable.

Numbers need not measure wisdom. The lesson’s inventory of books and resources is a teaching comparison, not a historical census of Euthydemus’s collection. Ordinals such as πρῶτος and δεύτερος decline as adjectives.

table.title: 3. Numbers and measured claims

sections.title: 4. ὡς and its compounds in context
body: ὡς has several uses; let the sentence determine the sense. With a comparison it can mean “as”; with a superlative, “as ... as possible.” ὥσπερ means “just as,” and ὥστε commonly introduces a result, often with an infinitive.
Do not force every ὡς into the English “that.” Here learn these reading patterns as units. Extended indirect statement and advanced clause systems belong to later lessons.

rows: so as to learn / with the result of learning

sections.title: Meet the Memorabilia: Euthydemus under examination
body: In Memorabilia 4.2, Euthydemus has collected writings and hopes for distinction. Socrates draws him into questions that expose the difference between possessing material and understanding what one can do with it. Our main selection is 4.2.24–30, with the earlier book-collecting context.

Think of the four books as a gallery of encounters rather than a continuous biography. Book 1 answers accusations against Socrates and presents his religious practice and daily conduct. Books 2–3 explore family, friendship, useful work, and leadership. Book 4 gives sustained attention to education, including the questioning of Euthydemus. The movement from an ordinary habit to a public responsibility is characteristic of the collection.

Xenophon writes as an advocate for a teacher condemned at Athens in 399 BCE. His Socrates improves other people through example, questions, and practical reasoning. That organizing purpose makes the work valuable evidence for an ancient interpretation of Socrates; it does not make every conversation a stenographic record. Notice who asks the questions, who changes position, and where the narrator supplies the judgment.

Reading invitation: open Book 1, chapter 5, then Book 4, chapter 5. Ask whether mastery of appetite is merely a rule about pleasure or a condition for learning and dependable action. Keep a small dossier of the different kinds of evidence Xenophon offers: reported speech, observed habit, analogy, and the narrator’s praise.

The dialogue turns to knowing oneself. Xenophon presents this as part of Socratic education: recognizing one’s capacities and limitations can affect choices and relationships. The conversation is a literary portrait, not a psychological test with a modern scoring scale.

sections.title: Books as objects, knowledge as work
body: A roll can be acquired and stored. Understanding requires reading, testing a claim, and applying it. The Reading banner’s rolls and tablet are modern visual suggestions of that difference; their number is not a census of Euthydemus’s collection. The Culture/History banner imagines Delphi, connecting the passage’s Delphic injunction to know oneself with the work of examining what one actually understands. It is not an archaeological plan of the sanctuary.

Make two lists: things a learner can own, and things a learner can do. Move “knowing a paradigm” to the second list only when you can use it to read an unfamiliar sentence. This is the lesson’s practical version of self-examination.

sections.title: Know thyself, precisely
body: The familiar Delphic maxim enters the discussion as a demand for examination. Here knowing oneself involves recognizing strengths and limits relevant to action, not merely stating a name or describing a mood.

Socrates’s questioning can be uncomfortable. Ask whether a question helps the learner see a real gap, and what support would help close it. Discovering ignorance is a beginning, not a complete teaching plan.

sections.title: Build a useful learning inventory
body: Choose one grammar skill you can perform without help, one you can perform with a table, and one you cannot yet explain. Give an example for each. This is evidence, not a ranking of your worth.
Use δηλῶ to explain what your example makes clear. Use a number for actual items counted, then say what the count cannot show. Ten completed exercises do not by themselves establish understanding.
